title: Circular Measure — Maths4U Original

provenance.basis: Independent skill briefs; no examination question supplied for paraphrasing.

marking_policy: Maths4U indicative marking guidance, not an official examination-board mark scheme. Award stated criteria once each, up to the part maximum. Accept valid equivalent methods. Follow-through applies only where explicitly stated; do not award an accuracy criterion for an incorrect final result.

lessons.title: Radians, degrees and complete rotations
lessons.objective: Convert angle units and distinguish a swept rotation from the final direction.
lessons.notes_html:
Before you start: work with fractions of a full turn and keep exact multiples of π.

One radian is the central angle subtended by an arc whose length equals the radius. In general \(\theta=s/r\), so \(2\pi\) radians make one complete turn and \(\pi\) radians equal \(180^\circ\).

\[\theta_{\mathrm{rad}}=\theta_{\mathrm{deg}}\frac{\pi}{180},\qquad \theta_{\mathrm{deg}}=\theta_{\mathrm{rad}}\frac{180}{\pi}.\]

A minor positive angle is less than π; a reflex angle is between π and 2π. The minor and reflex angles between the same two radii add to 2π. A physical rotation can exceed 2π: for distance travelled, retain every full revolution rather than reducing the angle to the final orientation.

Radian formulae require radian inputs. Keep π exact until the last numerical step and use radians in a calculator when evaluating trigonometric functions of radian angles.

Recall later

\(\pi/3\) rad = \(60^\circ\); \(450^\circ=5\pi/2\) rad is one full turn plus a quarter turn.

examples.solution_html: Multiply by π/180: \(150\pi/180=5\pi/6\) rad. This is less than π, as expected for an angle below 180°.
\((7\pi/4)(180/\pi)=315^\circ\). It is a reflex angle, between 180° and 360°.

examples.question_html: Two angles around a point are in the ratio 3:5 and sum to a full turn. Find both in radians.
examples.solution_html: Eight parts make 2π, so one part is π/4. The angles are \(3\pi/4\) and \(5\pi/4\), equivalent to 135° and 225°.

common_mistakes: Multiplying by 180/π when converting degrees to radians.
Using the minor angle when a reflex arc is specified.
Discarding complete turns in a travelled-distance calculation.

lessons.title: Arc length, sector perimeter and rolling distance
lessons.objective: Choose the correct arc and count every part of the required boundary.
lessons.notes_html:
Before you start: convert degrees to radians and distinguish radius from diameter.

For radius r and an angle θ in radians, the arc length is \(s=r\theta\). For a proper sector, \(0<\theta<2\pi\), its boundary consists of the arc and two radii:

\[P=2r+r\theta=r(2+\theta).\]

At a full circle the radial edges are not part of the outside boundary: its circumference is 2πr, not 2r+2πr. A chord is a straight segment; it cannot replace an arc in these formulae.

A wheel rolling without slipping travels one circumference per revolution. More generally, travelled distance is radius times total swept angle. With constant angular speed ω in rad/s, distance after t seconds is \(r\omega t\). Check that all lengths use compatible units.

Recall later

An arc of length 2.4 cm on a radius of 4 cm subtends \(\theta=2.4/4=0.6\) rad.

examples.question_html: For a sector of radius 6 cm and angle 0.8 rad, find arc length and perimeter.
examples.solution_html: The arc is \(6(0.8)=4.8\) cm. Its complete perimeter is \(4.8+2(6)=16.8\) cm.

examples.question_html: An arc has length 9 m on a circle of radius 3 m. Find its central angle.
examples.solution_html: \(\theta=s/r=9/3=3\) rad. The angle is not 3 degrees; the quotient of two compatible lengths defines radians.

examples.question_html: A wheel of radius 0.4 m rolls five complete revolutions without slipping. Find its travelled distance.
examples.solution_html: The total angle is \(10\pi\) rad, so distance \(=0.4(10\pi)=4\pi\) m, approximately 12.6 m to 3 significant figures.

common_mistakes: Giving only rθ when the question asks for sector perimeter.
Including two radii in the outside boundary of a full disk.
Using wheel diameter in place of radius in rθ.

lessons.title: Sector area and a fixed-perimeter constraint
lessons.objective: Use arc length and area together, then check a geometric maximum.
lessons.notes_html:
Before you start: rearrange an equation and complete a quadratic square.

A sector takes the fraction θ/(2π) of a disk, giving

\[A=\frac12r^2\theta=\frac12rs,\qquad s=r\theta.\]

Use radians and squared length units. The formula gives the ordinary sector area for angles up to one turn. For a sweep beyond 2π it counts repeated coverage, not the distinct area of the disk.

If a proper sector has fixed perimeter L, then \(\theta=L/r-2\) and \(A=Lr/2-r^2\). Complete the square to locate a maximum, then check that its radius is positive and its angle lies strictly between 0 and 2π.

Recall later

A sector with r=4 cm and θ=0.75 rad has area \(\frac12(16)(0.75)=6\text{ cm}^2\).

examples.question_html: Find the area of a sector with radius 5 cm and angle 1.2 rad.
examples.solution_html: \(A=\frac12(5^2)(1.2)=15\text{ cm}^2\). The square is on the radius, not on the angle.

examples.question_html: A sector has area 30 cm² and arc length 10 cm. Find r and θ.
A proper sector has perimeter 20 cm. Find its largest area.
examples.solution_html: \(A=10r-r^2=25-(r-5)^2\), so the maximum is 25 cm² at r=5 cm. Its angle is \(20/5-2=2\) rad, which is permitted.

common_mistakes: Using radius rather than radius squared in the area formula.
Accepting an algebraic maximum without checking the sector angle.

lessons.title: Chords, minor segments and major segments
lessons.objective: Subtract a triangle from a sector and identify the required curved region.
lessons.notes_html:
Before you start: use basic triangle trigonometry and set the calculator to radians.

A segment is bounded by a chord and an arc. For the minor central angle \(0<\theta\le\pi\), its area is sector minus triangle:

\[A_{\mathrm{minor}}=\frac12r^2(\theta-\sin\theta).\]

The chord length is \(c=2r\sin(\theta/2)\). A minor segment perimeter is the minor arc plus the chord, not two radii plus an arc. The major segment area is \(\pi r^2-A_{\mathrm{minor}}\).

If a chord is perpendicular distance d from the centre, its half-length is \(\sqrt{r^2-d^2}\), and its minor angle is \(2\arccos(d/r)\). Keep the unrounded angle in later area calculations. Check that the requested region is minor or major before subtracting.

Recall later

For a diameter chord, θ=π and the triangle area is zero; either segment is a semicircle of area \(\pi r^2/2\).

examples.question_html: Find the minor segment area for r=4 cm and θ=π/2.
examples.solution_html: The sector area is 4π cm² and the triangle area is 8 cm². The segment area is \(4\pi-8\text{ cm}^2\). Its boundary length is \(2\pi+4\sqrt2\) cm.

examples.question_html: Find the minor segment area for r=6 cm and θ=0.9 rad.
examples.solution_html: \(A=18(0.9-\sin0.9)\text{ cm}^2\), approximately \(2.10\text{ cm}^2\) to 3 significant figures. The sine must be evaluated in radians.

examples.question_html: Find the major segment area when r=3 cm and the minor angle is 2π/3.
examples.solution_html: The minor sector area is 3π and its triangle area is \(9\sqrt3/4\). Subtract the minor segment from the disk to obtain \(6\pi+9\sqrt3/4\text{ cm}^2\).

common_mistakes: Subtracting a triangle from the wrong sector.
Using the minor angle but reporting its area as the major segment.
Using degrees in sin θ after substituting a radian angle.

lessons.title: Annular sectors and composite boundaries
lessons.objective: Add areas and trace only the exposed boundary of a composite region.
lessons.notes_html:
Before you start: find sector and rectangle areas, and distinguish an internal join from an outside edge.

An annular sector lies between radii R and r, with \(0 \[A=\frac12(R^2-r^2)\theta,\qquad P=(R+r)\theta+2(R-r).\]

A complete annulus has no exposed radial connectors. For a rectangle topped by a semicircle, the shared diameter is internal: count the bottom, two vertical sides and semicircular arc. Its area still includes both pieces.

Under an enlargement of factor k>0, all lengths and perimeters multiply by k, areas multiply by k², and angles do not change.

Recall later

For R=5 cm, r=3 cm and θ=1 rad, annular-sector area is 8 cm² and perimeter is 12 cm.

examples.question_html: Find area and perimeter for an annular sector with R=6 cm, r=2 cm and θ=0.7 rad.
A rectangle of width 6 cm and height 4 cm is topped by a semicircle of radius 3 cm. Find outside perimeter and total area.
examples.solution_html: The exposed perimeter is \(2(4)+6+3\pi=14+3\pi\) cm. The shared diameter is not counted again. The area is \(6(4)+\frac12\pi(3^2)=24+9\pi/2\text{ cm}^2\).

examples.question_html: The annular sector in example 1 is enlarged by factor 3. Find its new area, perimeter and angle.
examples.solution_html: The area becomes \(9(11.2)=100.8\text{ cm}^2\), and the perimeter becomes \(3(13.6)=40.8\) cm. Its angle remains 0.7 rad.

common_mistakes: Counting the shared diameter as an outside edge.
Using two full outer radii for the straight edges of an annular sector.
Multiplying area by k instead of k² under enlargement.

problems.title: A reflex arc followed by an extra turn
problems.objective: Convert exact angles and retain a complete revolution in a travelled distance.
problems.stem_html: A circle has centre O and radius 5 cm. The minor angle AOB is \(144^\circ\).
problems.hint_html: The reflex angle is 360° minus the minor angle. An additional revolution adds 2π radians to the swept angle.

parts.prompt_html: Find the minor and reflex angles AOB in radians, exactly.
parts.solution_html: The minor angle is 144π/180=4π/5. The reflex angle is 2π−4π/5=6π/5 rad.

criteria.requirement: Convert the minor angle to 4π/5 rad.

parts.alternative_methods: Converting the reflex angle 216° directly is accepted.
parts.common_error: Using 144 as a radian angle.
parts.label: a

parts.prompt_html: Find the length of the minor arc AB.
parts.solution_html: Use the minor angle: s=rθ=5(4π/5)=4π cm.

criteria.requirement: Use arc length rθ with the minor angle in radians.

parts.alternative_methods: Taking 144/360 of the circumference is accepted.
parts.common_error: Using the reflex angle for the minor arc.
parts.label: b

parts.prompt_html: A bead follows the reflex arc from A to B and then makes one additional complete revolution in the same direction. Find its total swept angle and travelled distance.
parts.solution_html: The swept angle is 6π/5+2π=16π/5, which exceeds one full turn. The travelled distance is 5(16π/5)=16π cm. Reducing the angle to its final direction would lose one revolution of travel.

criteria.requirement: Include the additional full turn in the total angle.

parts.alternative_methods: Adding the reflex arc length 6π cm to the circumference 10π cm is accepted, with the swept angle stated.
parts.common_error: Reducing the swept angle modulo 2π before finding travelled distance.
parts.label: c

problems.title: Three angles around a point
problems.objective: Solve a radian-angle equation and interpret a reflex angle in degrees.
problems.stem_html: Three non-overlapping angles around a point are \(\alpha=(3k+1)\) rad, \(\beta=(k-1)\) rad and \(\pi/3\) rad, where k is real. Together they make one complete turn.
problems.hint_html: The total is 2π radians. The constant terms in α+β cancel.

parts.prompt_html: Find k exactly.
parts.alternative_methods: A correct rearrangement of the angle-sum equation is accepted.
parts.common_error: Setting the sum equal to 360 while retaining radian expressions.
parts.label: a

parts.prompt_html: Find α and β exactly in radians, and verify that β is positive.
parts.solution_html: Substitution gives α=5π/4+1 and β=5π/12−1. Since 5π/12≈1.309, β≈0.309 rad is positive. Both are valid angle sizes in the partition.

criteria.requirement: Justify that β>0, for example with a controlled numerical comparison.

parts.alternative_methods: An exact comparison 5π>12 is accepted.
parts.common_error: Accepting a negative angle in the specified non-overlapping partition.
parts.label: b

parts.prompt_html: Convert α to degrees to 3 significant figures, and classify it.
parts.solution_html: α in degrees is (5π/4+1)(180/π)=225+180/π≈282.296°. To 3 significant figures this is 282°. It lies between 180° and 360°, so it is reflex.

criteria.requirement: Classify it as reflex using the appropriate interval.

parts.alternative_methods: The unrounded degree expression followed by correct rounding is accepted.
parts.common_error: Calling every positive angle below 360° a minor angle.
parts.label: c

problems.title: Changing the complete sector perimeter
problems.objective: Distinguish arc length from perimeter when applying a percentage change.
problems.stem_html: A proper sector has radius 9 cm and angle 1.2 rad.
problems.hint_html: The two straight radii do not change when only the angle changes.

parts.prompt_html: Find its arc length.

criteria.requirement: Use s=rθ with the given radian angle.

parts.alternative_methods: A correct fraction-of-circumference method is accepted.
parts.common_error: Multiplying by another π/180 despite the angle already being in radians.
parts.label: a

parts.prompt_html: Find its complete perimeter.

criteria.requirement: Include both radii as well as the arc.

parts.alternative_methods: Tracing the three boundary pieces is accepted.
parts.common_error: Counting only the curved edge.
parts.label: b

parts.prompt_html: The radius stays fixed, and the complete perimeter increases by 25%. Find the new angle.
parts.solution_html: The new perimeter is 1.25(28.8)=36 cm. The new arc length is 36−18=18 cm, so the angle is 18/9=2 rad. It is a valid proper-sector angle.

criteria.requirement: Calculate the new full perimeter 36 cm.
Remove the two fixed radii to obtain the new arc length.

parts.alternative_methods: Solving 9(2+θ)=36 directly is accepted.
parts.common_error: Increasing the angle by 25%, which would not increase the whole perimeter by 25%.
parts.label: c

problems.title: A wheel rolling at a constant rate
problems.objective: Connect degree rate, swept radians, distance and whole revolutions.
problems.stem_html: A wheel of radius 0.35 m rolls without slipping at a constant rate of \(120^\circ\) per second.
problems.hint_html: Convert the angular rate to radians per second before using distance=r×angle.

parts.prompt_html: Find its angular speed in radians per second, exactly.
parts.solution_html: 120π/180=2π/3 rad per second.
parts.alternative_methods: Using one third of a revolution per second is accepted.
parts.common_error: Giving a numerical angular speed with degree units after conversion.
parts.label: a

parts.prompt_html: Find the distance travelled in 18 seconds, exactly and to 3 significant figures.
parts.solution_html: The swept angle is (2π/3)(18)=12π rad. Distance=0.35(12π)=4.2π m≈13.2 m to 3 significant figures.

criteria.requirement: Use the total swept angle to obtain exact distance 4.2π m.

parts.alternative_methods: Six revolutions each of circumference 0.7π m is accepted.
parts.common_error: Using the final orientation after 18 seconds, which returns to its starting direction.
parts.label: b

parts.prompt_html: How long does the wheel take to travel \(28\pi\) m, and how many complete revolutions is this?
parts.solution_html: The circumference is 0.7π m, so the number of turns is 28π/(0.7π)=40. At one turn every 3 seconds the time is 120 s. Equivalently solve 0.35(2π/3)t=28π.

criteria.requirement: Use circumference or constant linear speed correctly.

parts.alternative_methods: Either distance/speed or revolutions/rate is accepted.
parts.common_error: Using 0.35π as the circumference.
parts.label: c

problems.title: Recovering a sector from its area and arc
problems.objective: Eliminate the angle and recover radius, perimeter and the disk fraction.
problems.stem_html: A proper sector has area 54 cm² and arc length 12 cm.
problems.hint_html: Combine A=r²θ/2 and s=rθ to obtain A=rs/2.

parts.prompt_html: Find its radius.
parts.solution_html: Since A=rs/2, 54=r(12)/2=6r. Hence r=9 cm.

criteria.requirement: Relate area and arc length using A=rs/2 or equivalent elimination.

parts.alternative_methods: A simultaneous solution of the two standard sector equations is accepted.
parts.common_error: Using the arc length as a perimeter or a diameter.
parts.label: a

parts.prompt_html: Find its angle in radians.
parts.solution_html: θ=s/r=12/9=4/3 rad, which is between 0 and 2π.

criteria.requirement: Use θ=s/r with the recovered radius.

parts.alternative_methods: Substitution into the sector-area formula is accepted.
parts.common_error: Using θ=r/s.
parts.label: b

parts.prompt_html: Find its complete perimeter and the fraction of its full disk occupied by the sector.
parts.solution_html: The perimeter is 12+2(9)=30 cm. The full disk area is 81π cm², so the fraction is 54/(81π)=2/(3π). This also equals θ/(2π).
parts.alternative_methods: Using the angle fraction θ/(2π) is accepted.
parts.common_error: Dividing the arc by radius and treating that radian angle as the fraction of a full disk.
parts.label: c

problems.title: The greatest area with a fixed boundary
problems.objective: Build a quadratic area model and check the angle at its maximum.
problems.stem_html: A proper sector has radius r cm, angle θ radians with \(0<\theta<2\pi\), and complete perimeter 24 cm.
problems.hint_html: The boundary includes two radii. Substitute the resulting angle into the area formula, then complete the square.

parts.prompt_html: Express θ in terms of r and show that the area is \(A=12r-r^2\) cm².
parts.alternative_methods: Eliminating arc length first is accepted.
parts.common_error: Setting the arc length alone equal to 24.
parts.label: a

parts.prompt_html: Find the maximum possible area and the corresponding radius.
parts.solution_html: A=36−(r−6)². The square is nonnegative, so no area exceeds 36 cm²; equality occurs at r=6 cm.

criteria.requirement: Use a valid quadratic maximum method.

parts.alternative_methods: Differentiation with a maximum justification is accepted.
parts.common_error: Finding the vertex radius but reporting it as the maximum area.
parts.label: b

parts.prompt_html: Find the angle at this maximum and verify that it satisfies the geometric conditions.
parts.solution_html: At r=6, θ=24/6−2=2 rad. The radius is positive and 0<2<2π, so the algebraic maximum is attained by a proper sector.

criteria.requirement: Check positive radius and a proper-sector angle strictly between 0 and 2π.

parts.alternative_methods: An equivalent explicit domain check is accepted.
parts.common_error: Assuming every algebraic vertex is a valid geometric region.
parts.label: c

problems.title: A segment with an exact central angle
problems.objective: Distinguish a segment area and boundary from those of its sector.
problems.stem_html: A chord AB subtends the minor angle \(\pi/3\) at the centre of a circle of radius 8 cm.
problems.hint_html: The chord has length 2r sin(θ/2). The segment is the sector with its central triangle removed.

parts.prompt_html: Find the minor arc length AB and the chord length AB exactly.
parts.solution_html: The arc is 8(π/3)=8π/3 cm. The chord is 16 sin(π/6)=8 cm.

criteria.requirement: Give chord length 8 cm using a correct triangle method.

parts.alternative_methods: The central triangle is equilateral, so the chord equals the radius; this is accepted.
parts.common_error: Treating the chord and arc as equal lengths.
parts.label: a

parts.prompt_html: Find the minor segment area exactly, and then to 3 significant figures.
parts.solution_html: The sector area is (1/2)(64)(π/3)=32π/3 cm². The triangle area is (1/2)(64)sin(π/3)=16√3 cm². Subtracting gives 32π/3−16√3≈5.79751 cm², or 5.80 cm² to 3 significant figures.

criteria.requirement: Obtain the correct sector and triangle areas.
Subtract to give the exact segment area 32π/3−16√3.
Give 5.80 cm² to 3 significant figures without premature rounding.

parts.alternative_methods: The direct minor-segment formula gives full credit when the exact expression and rounding are correct.
parts.common_error: Subtracting the triangle from the full disk instead of the minor sector.
parts.label: b

parts.prompt_html: Find the perimeter of this minor segment exactly.
parts.solution_html: The segment is bounded by the chord and the minor arc. Its perimeter is 8+8π/3 cm; the two radii are internal to this description and are not its boundary.
parts.alternative_methods: A clear boundary trace is accepted.
parts.common_error: Adding two radii as though the region were a sector.
parts.label: c

problems.title: From chord distance to a major segment
problems.objective: Recover a minor angle from a chord and take the correct area complement.
problems.stem_html: A circle has radius 5 cm. A chord is perpendicular distance 3 cm from its centre. Let θ be the minor central angle subtended by the chord.
problems.hint_html: The perpendicular from the centre bisects the chord. Compute the minor segment first, then subtract it from the disk.

parts.prompt_html: Find the chord length.
parts.solution_html: The half-chord is √(5²−3²)=4 cm, so the chord length is 8 cm.

criteria.requirement: Use Pythagoras to obtain half-chord 4 cm.
Double it to obtain chord length 8 cm.

parts.alternative_methods: An equivalent right-triangle calculation is accepted.
parts.common_error: Reporting the half-chord as the full chord.
parts.label: a

parts.prompt_html: Find θ in radians to 3 significant figures.
parts.solution_html: cos(θ/2)=3/5, so θ=2 arccos(3/5)≈1.854590436 rad. To 3 significant figures θ=1.85 rad; retain the unrounded value for part (c).

criteria.requirement: Use a correct half-angle trigonometric equation.
Give θ=1.85 rad to 3 significant figures.

parts.alternative_methods: Using θ=2 arcsin(4/5) is accepted.
parts.common_error: Returning only the half-angle or leaving a degree result labelled radians.
parts.label: b

parts.prompt_html: Find the major segment area to 3 significant figures.
parts.solution_html: The central triangle has area (1/2)(8)(3)=12 cm². The minor segment area is (25/2)θ−12. The major segment area is therefore 25π−(25/2)θ+12≈67.3574 cm², or 67.4 cm² to 3 significant figures.

criteria.requirement: Find the minor segment area by subtracting the triangle from its sector.
Take the complement in the full disk.

parts.alternative_methods: A correctly derived major-angle segment formula is accepted.
parts.common_error: Reporting the minor segment area as the requested major area.
parts.label: c

problems.title: Enlarging an annular sector
problems.objective: Count both arcs and radial connectors, then use area scale to find length scale.
problems.stem_html: An annular sector has inner radius 4 cm, outer radius 7 cm and angle 1.5 rad.
problems.hint_html: Subtract the two sector areas. The two straight edges each have length 7−4.

parts.prompt_html: Find its area.

criteria.requirement: Subtract the inner-sector area from the outer-sector area.

parts.alternative_methods: The equivalent factorised expression (1/2)(R−r)(R+r)θ is accepted.
parts.common_error: Subtracting radii before squaring rather than subtracting their squares.
parts.label: a

parts.prompt_html: Find its complete perimeter.
parts.solution_html: The arcs total (7+4)(1.5)=16.5 cm. The straight edges total 2(7−4)=6 cm. The complete perimeter is 22.5 cm.

criteria.requirement: Include both arcs and two thickness-length connectors.

parts.alternative_methods: Adding all four boundary pieces individually is accepted.
parts.common_error: Counting only the outer arc or using two whole outer radii.
parts.label: b

parts.prompt_html: A similar enlarged annular sector has area 99 cm². Find the enlargement factor, its perimeter and its angle.
parts.solution_html: The area ratio is 99/24.75=4, so the positive length scale is √4=2. Its perimeter is 2(22.5)=45 cm. Similarity preserves the angle, which remains 1.5 rad.

criteria.requirement: Obtain length scale 2 from the area ratio.

parts.alternative_methods: An equivalent radius-based similarity argument is accepted.
parts.common_error: Multiplying the perimeter or the angle by the area ratio 4.
parts.label: c

problems.title: A rectangle topped by a semicircle
problems.objective: Model an exposed boundary and change its height while keeping the curved top fixed.
problems.stem_html: A rectangle of width 2r cm and height 6 cm is topped by a semicircle of radius r cm along its upper edge. The shared diameter is internal. The complete outside perimeter is \((20+4\pi)\) cm.
problems.hint_html: Count the bottom, two vertical sides and semicircular arc. The shared diameter is not an extra outside edge.

parts.prompt_html: Find r.
parts.solution_html: The exposed perimeter is 12+2r+πr. Thus (2+π)r=8+4π=4(2+π), giving r=4 cm.
parts.alternative_methods: An explicitly labelled boundary sum is accepted.
parts.common_error: Counting the shared diameter in addition to the rectangle bottom.
parts.label: a

parts.prompt_html: Find the total area exactly.
parts.solution_html: The rectangle area is 8(6)=48 cm² and the semicircle area is (1/2)π(4²)=8π cm². Total area is 48+8π cm².

criteria.requirement: Add the correct rectangle and semicircle areas.

parts.alternative_methods: An equivalent factorised exact expression is accepted.
parts.common_error: Using a full-circle area for the curved top.
parts.label: b

parts.prompt_html: The radius stays fixed and the outside perimeter increases by 10% by changing only the rectangle height. Find the new height and new total area exactly.
parts.solution_html: The perimeter increase is (20+4π)/10=2+2π/5 cm. It is shared between the two vertical sides, so the height increases by 1+π/5. The new height is 7+π/5 cm. The area is then 8(7+π/5)+8π=56+48π/5 cm².

criteria.requirement: Relate the perimeter increase to twice the height increase.

parts.alternative_methods: Solving the new perimeter equation directly is accepted.
parts.common_error: Increasing every length by 10% even though the radius must remain fixed.
parts.label: c
